## Question 4_

       First, HCOL:
       EDVA will probably apply VA procedural law (Klaxon). What substantive law

will EDVA DCt apply? VA is a 2nd restatement state, so EDVA will weigh the relevant

states’ interests and the transaction’s “center of gravity,” or where most of the facts are.

Because the facts regarding the collision with TT’s drone are mostly in VA (some in

WV) and VA has an interest in governing conduct that occurs in its territory, EDVA will

probably apply VA law to the tort claim. It could have applied WV law (and perhaps seen

a significantly different outcome on the tort claim), but the fact that collision occurred

just over the border is insufficient to negate VA’s interests in governing conduct that

occurs in its territory (drone flights by its citizens and companies that do business within

its borders). EDVA will probably apply NY law to the shareholder’s derivative claim

because the company is publicly traded in New York, and NY has a similar interest in
governing the conduct of the companies that trade therein, particularly when that conduct

has a significant effect on their stock price. This is not the ideal outcome for CC, as VA’s

standards for punitive damages are plaintiff-friendly.

       (a) There are several grounds upon which our clients can move to dismiss under

Rule 12(b).

       SMJ isn’t one of them. There appears to be FQL because there in an embedded

question of federal law (definition of “mail delivery”). (Smith-Grable exception). If there

weren’t FQJ, there would still be DJ because complete diversity (VA v. NJ) and AIC >

75k.

       Personal jurisdiction is a grounds for dismissal as per Rule 12(b)(2). EDVA
piggybacks off CA’s long-arm statute via FRCP 4(k)(1)(a). It’s improbable that VA has

personal jurisdiction over the defendants. First, there’s a question as to whether the

concept of privity extends to personal jurisdiction. D&Os are in charge of the company,

but the company is publicly traded. I’ll proceed as though privity has no bearing on IPJ

questions regarding a company’s D&Os. D&Os here have insufficient minimal contacts

with the D, the forum (VA) and the subject matter (Intl. Shoe). The D&Os haven’t

personally purposefully availed themselves of VA law, they didn’t personally direct the

harm into the forum, and they couldn’t have expected to be haled into VA for the actions

of a company of which they are simply D&Os. That said, VA’s interest in providing

effective means of redress for its citizens is strong here, and the ease of getting

information and witnesses may be easier in VA than in NY.

       Venue is another ground for dismissal under §1391(b), as per Rule 12(b)(2),

because (1) defendants don’t reside in EDVA; (2) the events occurred in WDVA and

WV; (3) the action may be brought properly in other districts (WDVA, DNJ).

       Finally, while we could argue that TT has failed to state a claim, it’s likely that this

argument will be unsuccessful. TT must meet the pleading standard, but there’s a conflict

here: SCOVA says pleading standard is notice, SCOTUS says standard is

Twombley/Iqbal. VCOL problem. While it appears that TT has pled sufficiently to meet

both standards (the complaint appears to have successfully crossed the line from possible

to plausible even after crossing out legal conclusions), I’ll perform VCOL analysis here:

       York: Not outcome determinative, so use federal rule: Twiqbal.

       Hanna Majority: The SCOTUS rule is applicable (on point) and appears to be valid.
SCOTUS is interpreting a FRCP 8(a), and in so doing is probably acting appropriately

under REA, though it could be argued that the standard “abridges” a VA citizen’s

substantive right in other cases. Scalia would say it’s an easy call: SCOTUS’

interpretation of FRCP 8(a) is on point, so there’s no need to look at state law. Use

Twiqbal.

       Harlan Concurrence: No problems here. While CC is a big company, it appears

unlikely to modify its primary conduct to take advantage of the state rule. May use

Twiqbal.

       Ginsburg (Shady Grove/Walker): VA’s state law here appears “powerful” in that

it’s a marked departure from FRCP with serious consequences for litigants, and Ginsburg

would try hard to construe the federal rule narrowly. She would probably struggle to do
so however, as the rules are in direct conflict. Perhaps she would construe the federal rule

narrowly in just this case, and in so doing revive the post-Twombley perception that

plausibility pleading only applies to certain types of cases.

       (b) This claim will be much tougher to dismiss.

       As above, FQJ is present under Smith-Grable because embedded federal question

of “mail delivery.” If no FQJ, TT cannot bring the claim against CC because it doesn’t

satisfy AIC requirement for DJ.

       General IPJ. CC is “essentially at home” in VA because its VA operations are

sufficiently continuous and systematic (like Wal-Mart).

       Venue, proper under §1391(b)(1).

       It’s unlikely that the claim will be dismissed for failure to state a claim (FRCP

12(b)(6)). Because TT has pled adequately under both standards, the VCOL analysis is

the same as above.

       (d) Because the tort claim against the D&Os will probably be dismissed, this won’t

be necessary. If, however, that claim is not dismissed, we’ll argue that the parties were

joined improperly under FRCP 20(a)(2). While there is a common issue of fact (drone

flights conducted negligently), we have a strong argument that the claims are based on

different T/Os, and should be tried separately.

       (addtl.) Issue preclusion (on the same issues as in SS’s preclusion argument) may

play a role here. Though the parties are different and VA requires full mutuality,

interstate preclusion rules require that a subsequent state court give as much preclusive

effect to a rendering federal court’s judgment as a state court in the state in which the

rendering federal court sat would. The rendering court is in NY, and NY has no mutuality

requirement. EDVA DCt should apply NY state preclusion law and require no mutuality.

Q1 is your best work — genuinely case- and reading-specific — and Q3 leads with the right doctrine and establishes privity on the facts. What holds the answer back is not writing or breadth but three failures to run a taught procedure to completion: the interlocutory-appeal canvass in Q2 never happens, Q4's amount-in-controversy analysis is inverted at both ends with no §1367 discussion, and the partner's punitive-damages question is never answered. ## Question 1

SMJ
No SMJ through AUJ: no embedded federal question (Mottley) and no crucial embedded
federal issue (Smith-Grable).

Look to Diversity, with requirement for complete diversity. HGInc. domiciled by place of
incorporation (MA) and PPoB (MA). Droobles domiciled in NH. Issue is Riddle, who
may be domiciled in RI or MA. Riddle born in RI, maintains RI voter registration, and

If Riddle kicked out for lack of SMJ, no sufficient AIC for suit against Droobles

for SMJ, look to whether Droobles can be joined through supplemental jurisdiction since

plaintiff against a party joined by Rule 20(a)(2).

PJ
No general IPJ over Droobles in MA or over Riddle if domiciled in RI: there is general

IPJ over Riddle if domiciled in MA, but then suit kicked out for SMJ.

Specific IPJ if long-arm to limits of Constitution and DP through minimum contacts and
traditional notions of fair play (International Shoe). 4(k)(1)(a) says FDC uses long-arm of
state in which it sits: MA has valid long-arm.

Probably fine for Riddle: offer for purchase received in MA, has MA office, and conducts

Less sure for Droobles: no advertising in MA so unlikely he targeted sales in MA (J.

solicitation. Suggests no IPJ over Droobles: can dismiss.

Venue
No venue under 1391(a): Droobles and Riddle not domiciled in same state. Look to

1391(b).

Substantial portion of events occurred in MA: gum taste test, receipt of emails, and
receipt of business valuations (last act for Tort purposes). Relies on court determining
that an email is where a person receives it: within realm of possibility. If website
constitutes property, could argue that website exists where content is created and
uploaded. Since HG creates all content, property impacted in suit could reasonably be in
MA. Likely cannot dismiss for lack of venue.

If MA not valid under 1391(b), couldn't use 1391(c) since venue also proper in NH.

Pleading

Likely cannot dismiss for failure to state a claim. Under Twiqbal, remove conclusory
statements and determine plausibility of remaining facts. Complaint alleges with
specificity via email that meeting at Droobles estate occurred, that HG received repeated
emails from Riddle including threat to reduce value of company, that HG has never been

were not provided, these are not adequate preliminary facts--this is unlikely.

No substantial policy reasons to dismiss case for failure to plead: unlikely to be a high-
cost discovery case since all companies are small and complaint deals with short time
period.

Notice and Service of Process
Service likely sufficient, since Droobles and attorneys received complaint.

Discrepancy between FRCP and MARCP. Erie analysis to determine whether motion to
dismiss for failure to provide separate document satisfying MARCP 4(a)(1)(h).

York outcome-determinative says MARCP results in dismissal while FRCP does not, so
use MARCP. Harlan says how lawyers file and notify unlikely to impact pre-litigation

conduct, so use FRCP. Under Scalia, FRCP valid since it doesn't "abridge, enlarge, or
modify" a state substantive right (permissible under REA) and applicable since it "really
regulates procedure" (Shady Grove): use FRCP. Under Ginsburg, FRCP valid under REA
but not applicable since no actual conflict: FRCP more permissive than MARCP and
doesn't bar additional requirements listed in MARCP 4(a)(1)(h), so use MARCP.

If following York or Ginsburg, dismiss. If following Harlan or Scalia, no dismissal for
failure to provide additional sheet unless other elements of FRCP 4(a)(1) not met.

## Question 6_

Claim preclusion: add that all dismissals (including for FNC, SMJ, PJ, and venue) are
now on-the-merits. Expansion of preclusion will likely increase efficiency but decrease
fairness to those who lack sophisticated understanding of court system.

Such a policy would support judicial efficiency by reducing refilings and dismissing
current cases. Parties would be incentivized to bring all claims at once, preventing future
suits and expediting decision-making. There's social benefit in having cases consolidated:
expedites restitution and helps parties to move on. Parties would also be discouraged
from filing frivolous lawsuits designed to harass defendants and instead focus on the
merits of the case. Parties would be encouraged to abstain from forum shopping for fear
of dismissal. This would also push more cases into state court, as parties wouldn't want to

risk having improper SMJ. This would support federalism, state adjudication of state
issues, and equitable administration of laws within the same region. Making permissive
counterclaims compulsory would encourage plaintiffs to research prior to filing to gain a
complete picture. Keeping cases in state court could be beneficial to plaintiffs--
particularly middle and low-income individuals--since federal courts tend to be more
favorable to big corporations.

The scheme also meets Vitek factors since it leaves intact the right to the first trial and all

associated due process protections.

The policy could be seen as balancing power between plaintiff and defendant, since
plaintiff would be held to a higher standard of review and would be subject to
consequences for mistakes that arguably should be corrected prior to filing. Could also

incentivize corporations to choose FSCs that don't fight the public interest.

However, such a policy would be unfair--particularly for pro se clients without
knowledge of FRCP. Since the complexity of FRCP favors large corporations and those
who can afford expensive counsel, adding more procedural dismissals to the "on-the-
merits" category could incentivize crafty lawyering on behalf of defendants to get more
cases dismissed with prejudice through purely procedural means. A particular issue
would be with hidden FSCs: claims against corporations would be dismissed by the
handful because it's likely many plaintiffs are unaware they've even signed an FSC or that
the clause will not be challenged despite unconscionability or unfair bargaining practices.
Challenging to seriously argue that plaintiffs should have their suit claim-precluded

simply because they poorly interpreted FRCP or didn't know about a claim they could
have filed.

Requiring all permissive counterclaims could lead to issues under Twiqbal, where
plaintiffs are unable to plead with enough specificity prior to discovery to prevent these
cases from being dismissed.

Including FNC in this proposal would give judges even more discretionary power, since

they would have the ability to dismiss a case forever simply because they thought it could
be better adjudicated elsewhere.

These two desires would also likely clash: parties could be obligated to abandon
legitimate permissible claims for fear of disrupting SMJ, PJ, or venue.

When weighing these policies, Eldridge test tells us that private interest in having chance
to correct mistakes and reserve right to sue probably doesn't outweigh government
interest in efficiency. Unlikely to cause too much erroneous deprivation; scheme still
allows full case in front of a judge with opportunity to present evidence.

Could mitigate issues by simplifying FRCP for SMJ, PJ, and venue. Removal of AIC
requirements would allow more cases into federal court but make DJ easier to understand.
Removal of DJ entirely would simplify the boundary between state and federal court and
speed up growth of state law development. This is unlikely to prejudice out-of-state
defendants: frequent movement obviates distinction between in-state and out-of-state.

Could also mitigate issues by providing access to counsel (unlikely by Lassiter/Turner
precedent and fact that plaintiff would be receiving counsel) or providing non-counsel
safeguards like simple guides to FRCP, non-lawyer advocates to explain and guide
plaintiffs, or online filing that explains potential consequences prior to submitting file.

## Question 4_

All states here use same claim preclusion law, so an inter system analysis is not needed
for claim preclusion. Harry will probably be claim precluded. It's the exact same claim,

Answer-to-Question-__6_

Additional proposed rule: Remove the Parklane factor of plaintiff ease of joining L1 in
applying ONMCE. So now, the fact that P2 could have easily intervened in L1 is
irrelevant to determining whether they could exercise ONMCE in L2 against D1. The
policy interest here may be in not coercing additional potential plaintiffs into intervening
in litigation they may not want to, for fear of having to re litigate a contentious or
expensive issue should they choose to bring a subsequent suit.

The primary advantages of the first (the exam's) proposal would be judicial efficiency in
subsequent suits and greater finality. If more issues are disposed of in L1, fewer resources
need to be spent down the line in hearing these issues. There's even more resource-saving
if we can preclude issues upon which no time or effort was spent at all. All parties still
had their day in court, so the rule seems equitable. What's more, If rules around raising
particular issues and defenses during L1 were loosened (for example, loosening the
immutability of the pre-trial order), there would be an even stronger argument that the
parties had sufficient opportunities to have issues heard in the initial litigation.

However, there are many more downsides. There would ironically be a loss of efficiency
for the initial litigation, as the parties would now be incentivized to raise every possible
issue, as this will always be more strategically desirable than losing on every one by

default. One could also make a due process argument that an issue warrants its own day
in court, analogous to parties. Losses in court will become much more severe and far-
reaching to the losing party if they don't raise issues, perhaps functionally depriving them
of rights further down the road. This system will also advantage wealth and experience
with the legal system even more than at present, as good lawyering in recognizing every
potential issue becomes vital. Even if you may have easily won on the merits of an issue
in L2, you will lose if your attorney failed to raise it in L1. Indeed, corporations and other
repeat players in the legal system will easily pick up which issues they must routinely
raise, while everyone else will be disadvantaged. Preclusion doctrine is obscure enough to
where one would need an actual attorney, not just an expert of some type (see Powell in
Vitek) to navigate it. Litigation will also cost more if there are more issues to adjudicate.

The second proposed rule would make it easier to apply ONMCE, as a party could now
do so even if they could have joined the original litigation. Any expansion of ONMCE
has some clear general issues. It would encourage potential plaintiffs to sit on the
sidelines of litigation. Though we may be concerned about not forcing a party to join, we
are probably more concerned with efficiency in consolidating lawsuits when possible. On
top of this, the threat of ONMCE would make defendants much more likely to settle in
order to avoid any final judgment that subsequent plaintiffs could use against them.
Though we generally want parties to settle for the sake of judicial efficiency, there should
be some concern over the power imbalance that is created. Circumstances may arise
where the defendant is willing to pay exorbitantly more than P1 may individually be
justly owed, as P1 has outsized bargaining power when D1 is threatened by the specter of
many more subsequent plaintiffs using a ruling against it.

However, it is more likely that since Harry, Ginny, and other stakeholders of HG all lost money due to reputation loss, despite different stakes, Harry and Ginny are representative and aggrieved in the same way, with people not likely precluded.

23(b)

Not likely limited fund restriction since more for bankruptcy cases where only certain amount of money that D can pay so runs out. Not a structural 23(b)(2) case seeking injunctive relief. Likely falls under damages class actions.

Damages

Superiority

If million$ considered large individual claim, class action not needed. If considered small, likely needed and superior. Class member interests are similar so likely superior. However, HCOl differences in state law might make better for individual suits.

6.

Expanding claim preclusion to any claims that could have been brought in the first case would create many sweeping changes. In favor of expanding CP, judicial resources would be conserved even further. If you can’t try another case for similar reasons, then P is incentivized to bring in all evidence at once and finality will make it so the court will not waste money on cases with a similar result or using the same evidence. Lawyers will have fewer lawsuits so either get paid more per lawsuit or become less relevant in general. We can prevent the P from pestering the D with numerous, often frivolous lawsuits. If P will forum shop, we can ensure that they choose the forum of their liking.

However, expanding CP to any claims that could have been brought up in the first case also creates many issues. Those who cannot afford a lawyer or an adequate lawyer will face severe access to justice problems. In criminal cases, those who are falsely convicted will not be able to bring in new discovered evidence and will therefore remain wrongfully convicted. With public defenders being stacked against the D.A., police evidence, and public sentiment to crack down on crime, defendants are likely to lose. Since defendants will be more likely to rely on public defenders, and public defenders are overworked already, the issue of false convictions will severely worsen. One possible alternative is that cities will hire more public defenders to stop the increased urgency of false convictions, but this is unlikely.

In civil cases, those who cannot afford an adequate lawyer will probably be more likely to lose a case since those with money can hire expensive firm lawyers to gather all of this evidence through discovery and the lawyers that defendants have will not be able to compete and be more likely to lose the case. In our unequal capitalist society, those with less money will face further hardships, deepening inequality. However, one could argue that for civil cases, the urgency of finality in expanding CP would help non-lawyers become more active in representing people, civil right to counsel could become a possibility, or know your rights programs would become more common for pro se litigants to defend themselves more accurately, especially considering the high rate of pro se litigants in general in civil suits. Still, it isn’t likely that these positive outcomes would come from expanding CP. It is more likely that the negatives would expand. For example, cities might try and blanket target people for tickets or other simple quality of life offenses to continue making money off of them. Since many low-SES and POC will not be able to win their cases, the cities will reap huge financial profits with little incentive to do otherwise. Therefore, marginalized communities would likely become more over-policed and marginalized in general.

## Question 1

SMJ:

       No AUJ: No Federal COA. No imbedded Federal issue, so no smith-grable

exception.

       No DJ: Insufficient AIC, so no DJ. Citizenship: HG=MA(PPoB & Place of
Incorporation). DD is a citizen of NH. However, AIC is only $50k.

       SJ: Maybe there's SJ because this claim ("Claim 2," against DD) is from the same
case/controversy as Claim 1 (against TMR). Since SJ has to be anchored by Claim 1, we
first analyze SMJ over the Claim 1.

SMJ over Claim 1:

       No AUJ: No Federal COA. No imbedded Federal issue, so no smith-grable
exception.

       DJ: Probably yes. $950k AIC is sufficient, and parties are probably diverse.
Citizenship: HG=MA(PPoB & Place of Incorporation). TMR is probably domiciled in
RI. Although TMR bought an apartment in MA and pays MA tax, he still returns to his
RI home every weekend (and he votes in RI). Buying an apartment and paying taxes in
MA is probably insufficient to change where he's domiciled since he returns to his RI

residence every weekend (Mas v. Perry).

IPJ: We should look at IPJ over TMR too because the Court might decline to exercise SJ
over Claim 2 if Claim 1 (the anchoring claim) got dismissed (1367(c)(4)).

General IPJ: No general IPJ over either TMR or DD. GenIPJ over TMR only if he's an
MA citizen (probably not, discussion in DJ). TMR has systemic and continuous presence
in MA (Shoe, Perkins), but General IPJ based on continuous presence probably does not
apply to individuals. No GenIPJ over DD. He's a NH citizen.

Specific IPJ: There might be specific IPJ over both TMR and DD(Calder v. Jones, but
see Griffis v. Luban). HG can argue that TMR and DD intentionally aimed their tortious
conduct to MA residents, so there should be specific IPJ (Calder). MA was the focal
point of HG's injury. HG's main audience is probably MA residence since all of the
photographs and videos Harry makes feature MA landmarks. However, TMR and DD
can argue that mere knowledge that HG and its audience resides in MA is not sufficient to

establish that the defamation was directed at MA residents (Griffis).

Venue: Probably proper under 1391(b)(2). Venue would be proper under b1 if TMR is an
MA residence (but probably not). Not proper under b3 (venue would be proper in RI/NH
court). The loss of value of HG occurs in MA, and this is "a substantial part of the events
giving rise to the claim" (last event necessary). So, proper under 1391(b)(2).

Failure to State a Claim: Under Twiqbal plausibility pleading, we must establish

plausibility with sufficient factual support, striking out conclusory statements. The
complaint states a claim with sufficient specificty. We ignore ¶14 and the last two
sentences of ¶20 for being conclusory. Analyze each element of Business Disparagement:
(i) Evidence of participation via anonymous email
(ii) Allegedly false video beacuse Harry never set foot at Drooble's estate (¶13)

(iii) Evidence of reputation harm via youtube video
(iv) Evidence of loss of value via drop in ads revenue
Complaint is nudged accross the line from possible to plausible.

4(a)(1): MARCP requires an additional paper with the address of the courthouse and a
description of the nearest public tranportation. FRCP does not require this. There's a
VCOL issue here. Hooray, Erie!

Under York, the difference would be outcome determinative for the whole suit. Apply
state law.

Under Harlan in Hanna, the difference probably will not affect anyone's pre-litigation
connduct. Apply FRCP.

Under Hanna majority/Scalia, Rule 4(a)(1) directly speaks to the question at issue
(applicable) and probably really regulate procedure (Sibbach). Therefore, it is valid under
the REA. Apply FRCP.

Under Walker/Ginsburg analysis, we can narrowly construe FRCP 4(1)(a) as merely

setting a minimum requirement, but open to any additional requirements. MARCP
4(a)(1)(H) merely sets additional requirements not inconsistent with the FRCP.
Therefore, state law controls.

The Erie tests give mixed results. Dismiss if MARCP applies, otherwise probably not.

HCOL issue? Probably not because MARCP rule is clearly procedural for HCOL
purpose, so no need to do HCOL analysis here. Apply procedural law of the forum state
(MA).

## Question 2

TMR and DD probably met at their office. The email and mp4 are strong evidence
establishing the meeting between TMR and DD. Neither TMR or DD affirmatively
denied that they had a meeting (but they said they have no memory of it). However, HG
has no evidence regarding the modification of video.

(a)

HCOL issue is important here. If MA Public Access Defense ("PAD")applies, then DD's
summary judgment may be granted. Otherwise, no. Whether PAD applies is a substantive
law issue (not procedural), so apply NH HCOL rule (1st restatement). We apply the law
of the state where the last act necessary to complete the tort occured (lex loci deliciti).

The loss of value of HG occurs in MA, and this is last event necessary to complete the
tort of "Business Dispagaragement." So, MA substantive law applies and PAD can be
asserted.

Apply Celotex (Brennnan), first, to DD's motion. DD has the burden of persuasion at
trial because PAD is an affirmative defense. DD has to show that HG has "constant and
ready access to the public or media outlets." Can DD produce evidence that, if
unrebutted, would compel any reasonable jury finding in his favor? Probably yes. ¶6, 7,

which Harry himself testified for, are probably strong evidence that DD can assert PAD.
It's clear that HG has access to various media outlets (¶6). In addition, the fact that HG
can generate revenues from Ads is a strong evidence that HG as a significant number of
audience (¶7).

Now, burden of production shifts to HG. HG would have a hard time trying to show they
do not have constant and ready access to the public. Therefore, Summary Judgement for
DD based on PAD will probably be granted.

(b)

Apply Celotex (Brennnan) to HG's motion. HG has the burden of persuasion at trial to
show that DD and TMR are liable for Business Disparagement. Can HG produce
evidence that, if unrebutted, would compel any reasonable jury finding in his favor?
Probably no. HG can probably establish that a meeting occured between DD and TMR. In
addition, they may claim the YouTube video and TMR's "your company will be worth

less" statement evince that DD and TMR modified and distributed the false video.
However, that's not a very strong argument. A jury may reasonably believe that another
person obtained the mp4 without DD's or TMR's knowledge, modified it, and distributed
it (DD and TMR might have nothing to do with this). Therefore, HG's motion for
summary juddment will not succeed.

## Question 3

Not appealable. Damage has not been awarded. Not a final judgment, so not appealable
(Liberty Mutual). No injunction. No issue collateral to the merits. No trial Judge
recitation for double discretion 1292(b). No certification for Rule 54(b). No special harm
for mandamus.

-------------------------------------------

## Question 4

Claim Preclusion: Harry and Ginny are claim precluded.

         Same claim. The complaint by Harry and Ginny ("Ha&Gi") clearly assert the same
claim. That is, Business Disparagement based on Riddle/Harry deepfake video.

         Same party (in privity). Ha&Gi are in privity with HG (Gonzalez). Harry is the
CEO and the Chair of the Board. Ginny is the Vice President of the Board. They probably
exercised substantial control over the initial litigation ("L1") by HG. In addition, Ha&Gi
probably got some money from L1 settlement. So, their interest has been adequately
represented.

         Final Judgment on the Merit. L1 dismissal through settlement is probably
considered on the merit. First, as a policy matter, the interest of Ha&Gi was clearly
represented in L1. Second, the settlement with HG only makes sense if HG's shareholders
would be claim precluded. DD and TMR would be effectively paying double damage for
their tort if HG's shareholders are not claim precluded. Finally, the trial court issued a
judgment "with prejudice," indicating that the same claim should not be brought back to
court.

Issue Preclusion:

       Interstate Preclusion. The New Hampshire State Court should at least apply as
much preclusion as the court that renders the judgment in L1 (Semtek). However, which
one is the "rendering" court? MA or NH Fed Court? If the MA Fed Court was a Happy

Court, then a strong argument can be made that the transfer to NH Fed Court was merely
a change of courtroom. So, MA preclusion law should apply. However, a
counterargument can be made by applealing to simplicity. It'd be simpler if we can
determine the applicable preclusion law just by looking to the court that actually renders
the judgment. In this case, it's the NH Fed Court. So maybe NH preclusion law applies. If
MA Fed Court was the "rendering" court, then NH State Court need to apply no
mutuality for IP. Otherwise, apply NH strict mutuality requirement.

       Same issue. Clearly the same issue (Business Disparagement based on
Riddle/Harry deepfake video).

       Same parties. Not an issue if we're giving as much preclusive effect as MA IP law
(no mutuality). If NH law applies, then L2 does not have the same party as L1 (but can
we argue they're in privity, therefore the same "plaintiff"? maybe not), so no IP.

       Not actually litigated. The issue was not actually litigated in court. The parties
settled.

       May not be necessary to the decision. Unclear what motivates the settlement since

the discussion were not made public.

Therefore, no issue preclusion, but there's claim preclusion.

## Question 5

Under Rule 23, we need to consider four things:

- Commonality: Class members suffered the same injury (reduction in share value). The
claim depends on a common contention, that DD committed Business Disparagement,
capable of class wide resolution. Difference of damage awards to different members
should not be an issue here because it can be prorated. There might also be a different
HCOL issue here because plaintiffs are located in different states.

- Typicallity: Harry and Ginny have the same incentive as the other class members (to
get as much damage awards as they can).

- Representativeness: Harry and Ginny are probably representative. Although they own
more shares in the company compared to other members, this is probably insufficient to
cast doubt on their representativeness. Their interest is clearly alligned with other
shareholders here.

- Numerosity: Unclear because the number of class members is between 20 and 40. Is it
practicable for each member to bring their own lawsuit? probably. Each of the 1.5%
shareholders have $15k at stake here, so each of them can probably bring their own suit.

Plaintiffs are quite diverse (from four different states), so court are more likely to
consider the numerosity prong fulfilled.

Rule 23 requirements are probably met. This is a damages class action under 23(b)(3), so
there's two additional prong to fulfill.

- Superiorirty: All plaintiff have at least $15k of claim, so it's unclear whether a class
action is superior. Furthermore, there's might be a HCOL issue here because plaintiffs are
located in different states.

- Predominance: Common issue certainly predominate. See Commonality.

On balance, we can probably defeat class action by contesting
Commonality/Numerosity/Superiority.

## Question 6

       The first suggestion exapands issue preclusion by barring the losing party from
litigating an issue they could have raised in Litigation 1. This will surely promote
efficiency. By enforcing this rule, parties will not be able to "test out" their arguments in
multiple law suits. Rather, they will be incentivized to raise all issues and arguments to
win Litigation 1.

       However, the proposed rule face an issue more problematic than gratuitious
decision (Rios). Applying this new rule, it is entirely possible for a non-decision to have a
preclusive effect (even when the issue has never been litigated!). This is especially
problematic when combined with the lack of mutuality requirement (e.g. NY issue
preclusion law). If this new proposal were to be implemented, it has to be safe-guarded

by strict mutuality requirement. Non-mutual party should not be issue precluded just
because a different party in L1 did not raise the issue, especially if the non-mutual party
in L2 could not have joined L1. We need to make sure that a party had their full day in
court before precluding them (Marrese). Mutuality requirement will likely solve this
issue. As a policy matter, it's probably not unfair to issue preclude a party who chose not
to raise the relevant issue in the previous litigation.

       Furthermore, expanding preclusion rule can be burdensome for indigent litigant

since they might not understand complicated legal rules (Lassiter, Vitek). Applying this
rule, pro se litigants might be unjustly precluded in subsequent cases because they did not
bring up the relevant issue when they could have. One way to solve this problem is to
apply the new rule only to parties who are able to afford counsel.

         Another possible way to expand issue preclusion is to dispense with the "necessary
to the decision" requirement. This new rule would dispense with both the necessary and
finality element. For example, if an issue has been decided in Litigation #1, Court #2
adjudicating Litigation #2 need not wait until Litigation #1 goes to judgment to issue
preclude.

         Since litigation often takes a long time, dispensing with the "finality" requirement -
and by implication, the "necessary" requirement - can be beneficial, especially when an
important issue is decided relatively early. Under the current issue preclusion law,
subsequent courts are unable to use that decision to issue preclude because there's no
judgment yet. In contrast, under the new rule, subsequent courts do not have to wait for

L1 judgment to issue preclude. This will promote efficiency since litigation can take a
long time to reach judgment. In the meantime, other courts might be litigating the same
issue.

         However, there are significant drawbacks with this proposal. A decision on an issue
might be gratuitious (Rios), and we do not want gratuitious decision to preclude
subsequent litigants. In response to this criticism, it can be argued that if this proposed
rule is in place, courts - knowing that their decisions can be grounds for preclusion - will

no longer make "gratuitious" decision. Although, it is unclear if this response is
convincing. Furthermore, a decision regarding an issue might change during the course of
the litigation as new evidence comes to light. One possible way to mitigate this criticism
is by requiring that to have a preclusive effect, the decision has to be "reasonably certain"
and "unlikely to change."

       My proposed expansion of issue preclusion may be beneficial for pro se litigants.
Indigent litigants might not have the knowledge or resources to go to trial. By expanding
issue preclusion, pro se litigants can "piggy back" on others who have litigated the same
issue (even when there's no judgment yet). In addition, the proposal can be interpreted as
an attempt to simplify and "level down" our legal process (Turner). Removing the
"necessary to the decision" requirements for issue preclusion will make it easier for pro-
se litigants to use issue preclusion rules to their benefit.
